stories.summary: A friend starting a podcast asked Amit for advice because The Seen and the Unseen had done so well. He told her not to worry about what listeners find in episode one, but about what they will find to binge on by episode hundred. He also told her to make episodes that travel across time as well as geography, so they still make sense thirty years later. He frames this episode the same way: timely about the tariffs, but meant as a 'first draft of history' of a pivotal moment.
stories.insight: Content compounds. A body of work that stays relevant becomes a library people binge, and each new piece links into the rest. Amit calls this 'one long conversation', not a set of separate episodes.
stories.quote: do not think of what people will discover of the show in Episode one. Instead think of what they will discover in Episode Hundred and will be able to binge upon.

stories.topic: Hyundai knew more about cars than Tata Motors, and that's fine
stories.summary: When Hyundai built a car factory in India, the Indians who learned to make Hyundai cars picked up a new level of automobile technology and management. They then moved to Tata Motors, started ancillary firms and launched the next generation of EV projects. Hyundai later decided that all the small cars it sells worldwide would be made in India, which Ajay reads as proof of Indian manufacturing capability. He contrasts this with the Meiji Restoration, when Japan sent only a couple of thousand young people West. India sent far more abroad, and they learned mostly on the job before coming back.
stories.insight: The real payload of FDI is knowledge, and it walks out of the factory gate with the people who learned it. Ego about who is 'better' only gets in the way of that diffusion.
stories.quote: I have no shame in saying that Hyundai knew more about how to make cars than Tata Motors. There's no need for us to have arrogance or ego problems about it.

stories.topic: Twelve branches a year for all foreign banks combined
stories.summary: All foreign banks in India put together were allowed to open only twelve branches a year. In what was billed as a great liberalisation, the limit was raised to eighteen. Ajay asks why the state should come between an Indian customer who wants to bank with Citibank and Citibank. He calls this one of innumerable normalised pieces of Indian economic nationalism.
stories.insight: Economic nationalism mostly hurts Indians. Here it is Indian bank customers who lose out when foreign branches are rationed. Such rules also give Western populists ammunition against India.
stories.quote: Note all foreign banks put together were allowed to open twelve branches in India per year. And then in an act of great liberalization this went up to eighteen.

stories.topic: The map with no tankers in the Red Sea
stories.summary: A friend, Ashima Sharma, showed Ajay a world map with every one of the roughly 700 LNG tankers plotted as a dot. Not one was in the Red Sea. The Houthis are choking the route, and some ships pay them ransom to pass. Since 1945 the US Navy has run freedom of navigation operations as a global public good, but this time it has stepped back. For India this is huge, because the Suez route is the short way to Europe compared with going around the Cape of Good Hope.
stories.insight: The open trading system rested on a security guarantee nobody noticed. When the guarantee lapses, India's natural route to its natural market closes.
stories.quote: And there was not a single tanker in the Red Sea. There is just such a mind blowing moment for me.

stories.summary: At a conference Ajay and Ila Patnaik organised at NIPFP, a Chilean economist explained capital account convertibility with an analogy. You can be an 85-year-old who never leaves the house or eats out because you're scared of falling sick. Or you can be a 12-year-old who flies out the door, tumbles on the ground, plays with frogs and eats panipuri on the roadside. The child falls sick all the time but bounces back.
stories.insight: Resilience and autarky are opposite answers to a risky world. Ajay argues India's urge to hide behind high fences comes from insecurity. India has already rolled with the 1991 crisis, nuclear tests, Y2K, the Asian crisis and 2008.
stories.quote: Would you rather be the 12 year old flying out of the house when you wake up, tumbling on the ground, uh, consorting with frogs and eating panipuri on the roadside.

stories.topic: Arguing with Nitin Pai about kowtowing to Trump
stories.summary: Amit had lunch with Nitin Pai, Narendra Shenoy and Sudhir Sarnobat just after the first 25% tariff. The inside dope was that Trump would not have imposed it if Modi had simply agreed that Trump helped the India-Pakistan peace process. Pakistan had played along and nominated Trump for the Nobel Peace Prize. Amit argued Modi should kowtow if needed, since the tariff hurts both Indians and Americans. Nitin was completely against it. They remain friends.
stories.insight: The test for a leader is national welfare, not national ego. Pride is a cost paid by citizens, and Ajay's 'prosperity over pride' argument makes the same point.
stories.quote: if he had to kowtow then it's not a matter of ego or pride. You just do what's good for the country.

stories.topic: Reforms by stealth: 'You come back and sell them for me'
stories.summary: In the early 1990s, Gurcharan Das wrote to Manmohan Singh asking why he was doing reforms by stealth. Narasimha Rao and Manmohan Singh were selling the reforms as a better socialism that Nehru and Indira would have liked, when they were really a repudiation of socialism. Deng Xiaoping and Margaret Thatcher, by contrast, sold their reforms openly. Manmohan replied that Gurcharan should come back and sell them for him. Separately, Naushad Forbes told Amit that after a meeting with industrialists, Manmohan took him aside and asked him to say everything from the meeting in public.
stories.insight: Reform needs public salesmanship, and insiders often can't do it. That makes it the job of citizens and outside voices. Amit uses this to urge listeners who agree to be vocal.
stories.quote: And Manmohan said to him, You come back and sell them for me.

stories.summary: In June 1941, Germany invaded the USSR and pushed about a thousand kilometres into its industrial heartland. Under fire, the Soviets dismantled entire factories, moved them to Central Asia, reassembled them and restarted war production. Ajay suggests Indian firms facing a 50% US tariff think the same way: dismantle the factory and take it to a zero-tariff country like Sri Lanka.
stories.insight: Nimbleness can be a killer app. The assumption that a factory must stay where it was built is a mental block, not a law of nature.
stories.quote: That's how I feel today. That if there's a fifty percent tariff in India, dismantle the entire factory, take it to Sri Lanka.

stories.topic: How Vicks VapoRub became Ayurvedic, and every employee got a house
stories.summary: Gurcharan Das told Amit this story from his time as CEO of Richardson Vicks, around the early 1980s by Amit's reckoning. A new government levy on certain medicines threatened to make Vicks VapoRub unprofitable. In a crisis meeting, someone quietly pointed out that the formulation was compatible with Ayurveda, and Ayurveda wasn't taxed. Within 24 hours they filed it as an Ayurvedic rub. The bureaucrat saw what they were doing but it was within the letter of the law, so it passed. As an Ayurvedic product it could be sold at about four million outlets, including paanwalas, instead of about 50,000 medical shops. Gurcharan gave stock options to everyone down to the lowest peon, and the company registrar suspected a scam. The company lent money to staff who couldn't afford Rs 20 a share. Amit recalls the share price rising about forty times within a year, and every employee made a down payment on a house.
stories.insight: Indian firms can be remarkably nimble under bad policy. Amit doesn't celebrate jugaad, since firms shouldn't have to do it, but it gives him hope that Indian business can adapt to the tariff shock.
stories.quote: apparently if I remember correctly the share price within a year went up forty times and every employee of the company made a down payment on a house.

recommendations.item: The Long Road to Change (EIE Ep 36)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Ajay's framework for how the episode's ideas could become policy.
recommendations.reason: Change comes from shaping ideas and the climate of opinion upstream of policymakers, not from whispering to a joint secretary.

core_ideas.concept: Globalisation built India's best twenty years
core_ideas.explanation: Ajay calls 1991-2011 the biggest success in 5,000 years of Indian history: GDP grew about fourfold and hundreds of millions escaped poverty. The gains came through four channels once the Indian state got out of the way. Technology came in as machine tools, CPUs, operating systems, fibre and the internet. Knowledge came from Indians who studied and, above all, worked abroad and returned, and from foreign firms training Indians at home. Finance came from foreign capital, which backed the new economy before Indian investors did, and 'it was the foreigners that made Infosys great.' Markets came from abroad too: over 90% of Infosys revenue is foreign. Ajay's 'West' means liberal democracies, Japan, South Korea and Taiwan included.
core_ideas.quote: And that is simply the biggest shining success in 5,000 years of Indian history.

core_ideas.explanation: India's tech boom ran on global CPUs, Unix, TCP/IP and foreign database engines. Nobody demanded an Indian CPU or a subsidised chip fab. Ajay applies the same logic to today's calls for an Indian LLM. If Indian geniuses can help build a CPU, great; if not, buy other people's. The goal is progress, not owning the technology stack.

core_ideas.concept: Poverty is the default; growth is how people escape it
core_ideas.explanation: Amit points out that for most of history almost everyone was poor. Wealth arrived through technology and markets. Citing Lant Pritchett via EIE 57, every human welfare indicator has a 99% correlation with per capita GDP, and less than 1% with welfarism and redistribution. So GDP talk is a conversation about poor people's lives, and getting policy right is a moral imperative.
core_ideas.quote: People often look at economists as oh, they're talking numbers, they're talking GDP, what about the poor? Hello, we are talking about the poor.

core_ideas.concept: The end of the West's indulgence
core_ideas.explanation: India was never a good-faith player in the global system. Its officials spoiled trade talks, its rhetoric stayed anti-colonial, and unfairness to foreign firms was normal. Advanced democracies tolerated this, pushing deals through anyway and assuming India would grow up, since economic nationalism mostly hurts Indians. Right-wing populism across the West has ended that patience. China caused about 90% of the problem and India about 10%, but the rules have changed for both. Indian misbehaviour now feeds the politicians most hostile to India.
core_ideas.quote: So what we see with Trump today is to some extent made in India.

core_ideas.explanation: Trade between two countries works like Newton's gravity: it rises with the product of their GDPs and falls with the square of the distance between them. The US is huge but fairly inward-looking; India trades more as a share of GDP. It is also the farthest place India can ship goods, while China and Japan are a short hop across the Pacific. India's natural goods market is Europe via the Red Sea and Suez. Services escape gravity: photons on fibre are weightless, so California isn't far. That is why Indian services exports to the US thrive while goods struggle.
core_ideas.quote: it turns out that the trade between two countries is proportional to the product of their two GDPs divided by the distance between them squared.

core_ideas.concept: Tariffs hurt the country that imposes them, and India needs a healthy US
core_ideas.explanation: Amit is an anti-tariff absolutist: tariffs always hurt your own people. Ajay says the US damage is masked by a once-in-a-century AI capex boom, but it shows once you split out the Magnificent 7. He lists the harms: rising prices and unanchored inflation; uncertainty that chokes investment, making the US 'an emerging market'; cost shocks for US exporters who rely on imported inputs; and a fraying dollar safe haven. India should worry more about a faltering US than about the $65 billion hit. It relies on American finance, services demand, technology, GCCs and a Navy that keeps sea lanes open.
core_ideas.quote: The world needs a sound United States. India needs a sound United States.

core_ideas.concept: Shocks are absorbed by many small adjustments, but the window is still broken
core_ideas.explanation: Of about $460bn in Indian goods exports, about $85bn go to the US and about $65bn face the 50% tariff. That is roughly 15%, while $370bn of services exports are where the dynamism is. A $10 shirt becoming $15 looks like game over, yet the price system responds in several ways. Trade gets redirected: Vietnam takes the US order, and India picks up the German buyer Vietnam used to serve. The rupee depreciates. Firms absorb some margin, and workers move to other employers. Amit adds Hazlitt's broken window caveat: adjustment doesn't make the tariff harmless, because what is unseen is what would have happened without it.
core_ideas.quote: We should not think of it like throwing a switch and suddenly 65 billion dollars of exports is extinguished.

core_ideas.explanation: The US is only about a third of advanced-economy trade. The rest stays open: Western Europe, Canada, Chile, Australia, New Zealand, Japan, Taiwan, South Korea and Israel. These countries are rich and democratic, so treaties signed with them hold for five, ten or twenty years. Firms need that kind of horizon to invest. Strongmen rule by discretion and change their minds overnight, so businesses just wait and watch.
core_ideas.quote: So the problem in working with authoritarian countries is that strongmen are untrustworthy.

core_ideas.concept: Deep trade agreements and a new globalisation
core_ideas.explanation: The WTO failed because countries could cheat. A deep trade agreement (DTA) commits members to fair play across regulation, intellectual property, capital flows and foreign firms' right to operate, ruling out economic nationalism. The EU is the classic example. The TPP is another: when Trump walked out, the remaining 11 countries went ahead. Ajay wants India to help found a new coalition of 10-20 like-minded countries. He also wants India to start upgrading the UK FTA into a DTA now, since talks take two or three years, and to bring new imagination to deals with the EU and Japan. That means dropping third-worldism and the '500 red lines'.
core_ideas.quote: India can and should be a founder member of a new globalization.

core_ideas.concept: No red lines, no holy cows
core_ideas.explanation: In diplomacy, everything is negotiable at some price. Declaring agriculture off the table, as with the dairy barriers Trump targeted, throws away bargaining power. The Europeans don't get emotional about Trump; they play hardball and do deals. That makes fixing Indian agriculture at home a precondition for leverage abroad.
core_ideas.quote: once we adopt red lines, you basically stop doing diplomacy.

core_ideas.concept: What deep integration could look like
core_ideas.explanation: Ajay offers four concrete possibilities. German carmakers could build components, R&D and software in India. Japanese electronics firms, strong in design but now wary of China after it turned nationalist on them, could pair with Indian factories and engineers. South Korean shipbuilders under Chinese price pressure could combine their design skills with Indian production. In defence, Ukraine, Poland and South Korea are building frontier weapons at frugal prices, unlike 'gold plated' F-35s. India's southern cone could host R&D and factories far from Russian, North Korean and Chinese missiles. All of this requires India to drop oddities like curbs on royalties, capital movement and work visas. Along the way Ajay stresses that manufacturing jobs are high-skill, not unskilled assembly-line work.
core_ideas.quote: for a German company building in Belgium should be no different from building in India.

core_ideas.concept: Don't tax foreigners: a clean GST plus a carbon tax
core_ideas.explanation: Non-residents are not India's tax base, so exporters should get back every indirect tax paid along the supply chain (zero-rated GST). India's GST has 'birth defects': missing input tax credits and unrefunded cesses and electricity duties. Ajay sees the world converging on two taxes, a GST and an auditable carbon tax, that 'handshake' at the border. Under the EU's CBAM, carbon tax paid in India would be credited at Europe's border. He, Vijay Kelkar and Arvind Modi have argued for this design since the GST's early days.
core_ideas.quote: The price of goods on a ship on the high seas should be minus Indian taxation.

core_ideas.explanation: Every domestic fix ties back to winning the 66%. India's regulators have become a new central planning system and need fixing at the organisational source. Courts must work so a manufacturer facing strict penalties from a foreign buyer can pass them on to Indian vendors, and so foreigners can rely on contracts rather than caste and kin. Cities must work, because a 20,000-worker factory running three shifts needs about 60,000 households nearby. Finance must be able to fund $5-10bn complex projects, with players like Goldman Sachs in Bombay. Foreign firms need fair treatment through OECD-style tax treaties and bilateral investment treaties.
core_ideas.quote: Each of these points is directly connected to the project of Indian deep globalization so that we can do more with the sixty six so as to make up for the problems of the thirty three.

core_ideas.explanation: Autarky means hiding in a bunker; resilience means taking shocks and bouncing back. Ajay lists what resilience requires. First, fiscal prudence, since the debt-to-GDP ratio and primary deficit are too high. Second, an RBI devoted only to inflation targeting. Third, a genuinely floating rupee that falls instantly on bad news, which helps exporters. Fourth, deep, liquid markets and banks that don't blow up. The correct combination, he says, is an open capital account, inflation targeting and a floating exchange rate.
core_ideas.quote: A floating exchange rate is a shock absorber.

core_ideas.explanation: A tariff cut from 100 to 10 can always be reversed, so an announcement alone doesn't stabilise private decisions. Credibility comes from a visible team that understands the reform, an explanation of its full logic, and honesty about problems rather than propaganda. When the next crisis hits, the government needs that store of trust, so that people turn to Indian policymakers rather than the New York Times for the truth. A full rationale beats a fatwa handed down like the Ten Commandments.
core_ideas.quote: It is pouring concrete of credibility around the steps that were taken.

core_ideas.explanation: India can't do autarky with the US or China. With Trump, it needs deep expertise on MAGA and right-wing populism, and if flattery works, it should flatter. With China, 'Hindi-Chini bhai-bhai' won't do after Doklam, Galwan and Chinese overproduction. Instead India needs a brains trust that can get inside Xi Jinping's mind and work out the carrots and sticks. Twitter one-liners, autarky and 'strategic autonomy' serve moral purity, not the national interest.
core_ideas.quote: It is not a question of pride. It is a question of Indian self-interest.

core_ideas.explanation: Amit argues that trade games are either positive-sum or negative-sum. Treating them as zero-sum, for example by answering a 50% tariff with 60%, turns them into lose-lose. This reflex is the first of his three pessimisms. The second is that leaders find narrative battles, like the TikTok ban, easier than hard global work. The third is that the opposition opposes everything, and the small, mediocre elite clings to status-quo thinking.
core_ideas.quote: So any attempt at playing a zero sum game and doing one upmanship results, in my view, in a negative sum game.

core_ideas.concept: Theory of change: work upstream of the policymaker
core_ideas.explanation: Ajay argues that a joint secretary already has her own worldview and can hire KPMG or Bain to implement things, so advice offered downstream adds little. What shifts policy is new knowledge and a changed climate of opinion. The 1991 reforms came from thinkers who had spent years writing about what was wrong. Amit adds Andrew Breitbart's line that politics is downstream of culture, and says both mass culture and elite culture must change.
core_ideas.quote: For too many people in India, the theory of change is that somehow I will go whisper to the joint secretary, and the joint secretary will implement the reform.

core_ideas.explanation: Ajay's advice to firms has four parts. First, treat the US like an emerging market: be opportunistic and don't make long-term plans around it, since tariffs could swing from 50 to 300 and a Senate bill proposes 500% secondary oil tariffs. Second, tariff-hit American exporters may lose ground to Indian firms in markets like Belgium. Third, shift focus to the rest of the OECD. Fourth, be nimble, even to the point of moving a factory.
core_ideas.quote: Finally, in this fluctuating global environment, the race will go to the nimble.

jokes_and_cultural_references.content: After Ajay explains the gravity model, Amit concludes that 'the closer Ajay and I get to each other, the more likely we are to hug.' Ajay asks, 'And will there be a hugging black hole?' Amit backs off: 'I'm not going to be getting into very dangerous things.'
Ajay offers a free T-shirt to whoever binge-watches the most episodes in one weekend. Amit adds that the winner gets 'that shirt which you're wearing now, unwashed.'

Amit's detour into nihilism: 'No man is an island. Even though it must be said that every man is alone and will die realizing that life was meaningless and any sense of purpose was a mere illusion... Forget about searching for the truth, settle for a good illusion.'

When Amit turns pessimistic, Ajay says, 'You embody the mood of Bengali movies, but we should keep making more movies.' Amit fires back that 'you Gujaratis have a lot of responsibility for the state of the nation today, and I'm of course referring to Gandhi and Patel.'
Amit's pun on Ajay's call for nimbleness: 'if a firm should be nimble, why call it firm?'
After recounting his kowtowing argument with Nitin Pai, Amit cuts to a video of Nitin's reaction: he 'remains a friend. We survived that grievous incident.'
Ajay imagining the West's patience with India: 'As knowledge comes about in India, shows like EIE will come to India and the Indian side will gradually change.'
Amit's translation of the 'tapestry' of interlinked episodes: 'tapestry is really a fancy way of telling the gentle readers, binge watch, binge watch us.'
Ajay corrects himself after a YouTube commenter accused him of always saying electrons: on fibre optic cables 'it is photons that fly,' and they are weightless.
Smoot-Hawley: Ajay says Trump's tariffs are 'unheard of after Smoot-Hawley.'
Robert Lighthizer: the modern American right-wing voice whose arguments the hosts took seriously in their globalisation episodes, finding some 'rubbish' and some logic.
'We're not in Kansas anymore': Ajay's line for how much the world has changed, and why India must rethink from scratch.
The Meiji Restoration: Japan sent a couple of thousand young people West to study. Ajay says India's flow of people abroad and back was far bigger, and nobody made a fuss about it.
The Suez Canal and 'the glory of 1869': Ajay traces India's natural route to Europe via Gibraltar, the Mediterranean and the Red Sea, versus the long way around the Cape of Good Hope.
The Magnificent 7: Ajay says splitting them from the rest of the S&P 500 reveals the US pain hidden by the AI capex boom.
'Hindi-Chini bhai-bhai', Doklam and Galwan: Ajay's reminder that dealing with China can't rest on slogans after recent clashes.
The F-35: Ajay calls the American jet 'completely gold plated' to explain why frugal Ukrainian, Polish and South Korean defence partners suit India better.
The Ten Commandments: Ajay says that coming 'down from the mountain with the ten commandments' is worse policy communication than showing the full logic.
Andrew Breitbart's 'politics is downstream of culture', quoted by Amit to explain why think tanks targeting bureaucrats miss the point.
'Pessimism of the intellect, optimism of the will': the 'great line' Amit says he embodies, pessimistic about the world but still working to improve it.
Deng Xiaoping and Margaret Thatcher: the leaders Gurcharan Das held up as reformers who sold their ideas openly, unlike India's selling of reform as a better socialism that 'Nehru would have liked'.

The 1991-2011 statesmen: Amit names Narasimha Rao, Manmohan Singh, Chidambaram, Vajpayee, Jaswant Singh and Yashwant Sinha. He recalls cross-party cooperation, with Chidambaram and Jaitley talking and Sushma Swaraj advising UPA-1 on the new pension scheme.
